title: Hexadecimal, Decimal, Octal display
explanation:
Program 01: Number Base Conversion
Topic: Basic Input/Output

Reads an integer and prints it in three number bases using printf
format specifiers: %d (decimal), %x (hexadecimal), %o (octal). No
manual conversion logic is needed - the C standard library already
knows how to format an int in any of these bases.
output:
--- Program 01: Number Base Conversion ---
Enter the number: 689
Decimal format is     : 689
Hexadecimal format is : 2b1
Octal format is       : 1261

title: Largest and smallest among three numbers
explanation:
Program 02: Largest and Smallest of Three Numbers
Topic: Conditional Statements

Reads three numbers and uses two separate if-else if-else chains:
one to find the smallest (a number that is less than both others)
and one to find the largest (a number that is greater than both
others).
output:
--- Program 02: Largest and Smallest of Three Numbers ---
Enter three numbers: 4 7 2
2 is the smallest number
7 is the largest number

title: Class/grade based on marks
explanation:
Program 03: Class Based on Marks
Topic: Conditional Statements (if-else ladder)

Reads marks and checks them against descending grade bands (90+,
80-89, 60-79, 40-59, below 40) using an if-else-if ladder. Once a
condition matches, the rest of the ladder is skipped.
output:
--- Program 03: Class Based on Marks ---
Enter your marks: 89
Second class

title: Even or odd number
explanation:
Program 04: Even or Odd
Topic: Conditional Statements

Uses the modulus operator (%) to get the remainder when the number
is divided by 2. A remainder of 0 means the number is even,
otherwise it is odd.
output:
--- Program 04: Even or Odd ---
Enter your number: 9
Odd number

title: Leap year check
explanation:
Program 05: Leap Year Check
Topic: Conditional Statements

A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4 but not by 100,
UNLESS it is also divisible by 400 (e.g. 2000 is a leap year but
1900 is not). The condition combines both rules with && and ||.
output:
--- Program 05: Leap Year Check ---
Enter year: 1900
Not a leap year

title: Spellings of numbers 1-10
explanation:
Program 06: Number Spellings (1-10)
Topic: Switch Case + Functions

Reads a digit from 1 to 10 and uses a switch statement to print its
word form. Each case prints the matching word and breaks; any value
outside 1-10 falls through to the default case.
output:
--- Program 06: Number Spellings (1-10) ---
Enter number in digit: 9
Nine

title: Real roots of a quadratic equation
explanation:
Program 07: Roots of a Quadratic Equation
Topic: Conditional Statements + Math library

For ax^2 + bx + c = 0, the discriminant (b^2 - 4ac) tells us whether
real roots exist. If it is >= 0, the two roots are calculated with
the quadratic formula using sqrt() from <math.h>. If it is negative,
the roots are complex and the program says so instead of crashing.
output:
--- Program 07: Roots of a Quadratic Equation ---
Enter coefficients a, b, c: 1 -3 2
Real roots exist.
Root 1 is: 2.00
Root 2 is: 1.00

title: Prime check: single number OR a range
explanation:
Program 08: Prime Check
Topic: Loops + Functions

A number is prime if no integer from 2 up to its square root divides
it evenly (checking only up to the square root is enough, since a
larger factor would always pair with a smaller one already checked).
This program offers checking one number or scanning a whole range,
since both are really the same test applied once or repeatedly.
output:
--- Program 08: Prime Check ---
1. Check a single number
2. List primes in a range
Enter your choice: 2
Enter lower number: 2
Enter higher number: 10
Prime numbers between 2 and 10:
2
3
5
7

title: Print college name 20 times
explanation:
Program 09: Print College Name 20 Times
Topic: Loops

A simple for loop that counts from 1 to 20, printing the college
name once on each iteration.
output:
--- Program 09: Print College Name 20 Times ---
APC Roy Polytechnic
APC Roy Polytechnic
APC Roy Polytechnic
... (repeats to a total of 20 lines)
APC Roy Polytechnic

title: Menu driven arithmetic operations (switch)
explanation:
Program 10: Menu Driven Arithmetic
Topic: Switch Case

Reads a menu option and two numbers, then uses a switch statement to
perform addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division. Division
checks for a zero denominator first to avoid undefined behavior.
output:
--- Program 10: Menu Driven Arithmetic ---
1. Addition
2. Subtraction
3. Multiplication
4. Division
Enter your option: 1
Enter first number: 5
Enter second number: 4
Addition of two numbers is: 9

title: Swap two numbers using a third variable
explanation:
Program 11: Swap Using a Third Variable
Topic: Operators

The classic swap: copy 'a' into a temporary variable, copy 'b' into
'a', then copy the temporary value into 'b'. Simple and always safe,
at the cost of one extra variable.
output:
--- Program 11: Swap Using a Third Variable ---
Enter the value of a: 7
Enter the value of b: 3
Before swapping: a = 7, b = 3
After swapping : a = 3, b = 7

title: Swap two numbers without a third variable
explanation:
Program 12: Swap Without a Third Variable
Topic: Operators

Uses arithmetic instead of a temporary variable: a becomes a+b, then
b is recovered as (a+b)-b, then a is recovered as (a+b)-b(new). This
works but can overflow for very large numbers, unlike the
third-variable version.
output:
--- Program 12: Swap Without a Third Variable ---
Enter the value of a: 3
Enter the value of b: 2
Before swapping: a = 3, b = 2
After swapping : a = 2, b = 3

title: Swap two numbers using pointers
explanation:
Program 13: Swap Using Pointers
Topic: Pointers

Passes the addresses of a and b (&a, &b) into a swap() function that
takes int pointers. Inside the function, *x and *y dereference the
pointers to read/write the original variables directly - this is how
you make a function change the caller's variables in C, since C
otherwise passes arguments by value.
output:
--- Program 13: Swap Using Pointers ---
Enter the value of a: 10
Enter the value of b: 20
Before swapping: a = 10, b = 20
After swapping : a = 20, b = 10

title: Factorial (iterative)
explanation:
Program 14: Factorial (Iterative)
Topic: Loops

Multiplies fact by num, then decreases num by 1, repeating in a
while loop until num reaches 1. Negative numbers are rejected since
factorial is undefined for them.
output:
--- Program 14: Factorial (Iterative) ---
Enter the number: 5
Factorial of 5 is: 120

title: Factorial (recursive)
explanation:
Program 15: Factorial (Recursive)
Topic: Recursion

fact(num) calls itself with a smaller argument (num - 1) until it
hits the base case (num is 0 or 1), then the results multiply back
up the call chain: fact(5) = 5 * fact(4) = 5 * 4 * fact(3) ...
output:
--- Program 15: Factorial (Recursive) ---
Enter a number: 5
Factorial is: 120

title: Fibonacci series
explanation:
Program 16: Fibonacci Series
Topic: Loops

Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two before it (0, 1, 1, 2,
3, 5, ...). The program keeps two running values (t1, t2) and slides
them forward each iteration instead of recalculating from scratch.
output:
--- Program 16: Fibonacci Series ---
Enter number of terms: 8
Fibonacci series: 0 1 1 2 3 5 8 13

title: GCD and LCM of two numbers
explanation:
Program 17: GCD and LCM
Topic: Functions

GCD uses the Euclidean algorithm: repeatedly replace (a, b) with
(b, a mod b) until b becomes 0 - the remaining value of a is the
GCD. LCM is then derived from GCD using the identity
LCM(a,b) = (a / GCD(a,b)) * b, avoiding overflow from multiplying
a*b directly first.
output:
--- Program 17: GCD and LCM ---
Enter two numbers: 12 18
GCD is: 6
LCM is: 36

title: Armstrong check: single number OR a range
explanation:
Program 18: Armstrong Check
Topic: Loops + Functions

An Armstrong number equals the sum of its own digits, each raised to
the power of the digit count (e.g. 153 = 1^3 + 5^3 + 3^3). The
helper function extracts digits one at a time with % 10 and / 10.
Like Program 08, single-check and range-check are offered together
since they use the same underlying test.
output:
--- Program 18: Armstrong Check ---
1. Check a single number
2. List Armstrong numbers in a range
Enter your choice: 1
Enter the number: 153
153 is an Armstrong number

title: Sum of digits of a number
explanation:
Program 19: Sum of Digits
Topic: Loops

Repeatedly takes the last digit with num % 10, adds it to a running
sum, then removes that digit with num / 10, until num becomes 0.
output:
--- Program 19: Sum of Digits ---
Enter a number: 1234
Sum of all digits is: 10

title: Sum of numbers using an array
explanation:
Program 20: Sum of Numbers Using an Array
Topic: Arrays & Hashing

Reads n values into an array, then a for loop walks through the
array adding each element to a running total.
output:
--- Program 20: Sum of Numbers Using an Array ---
Enter the number of elements: 3
Enter the elements: 1 2 3
Sum is: 6

title: Smallest element of an array
explanation:
Program 21: Smallest Element of an Array
Topic: Arrays & Hashing

Starts by assuming the first element is the smallest, then compares
it against every other element, updating 'min' whenever a smaller
value is found.
output:
--- Program 21: Smallest Element of an Array ---
Enter how many elements you want to insert: 4
Enter elements: 4 5 6 2
Smallest element in this array is: 2

title: Find duplicates in an array using hashing
explanation:
Program 22: Find Duplicates Using Hashing
Topic: Arrays & Hashing

Instead of comparing every pair of elements (which takes O(n^2)
time), this keeps a "seen" array indexed by value itself: seen[v]
becomes 1 the first time value v is encountered. If a value is
already marked as seen, it is a duplicate. This "index by value"
trick is the core idea behind hash-based lookups, checking each
element in constant time instead of comparing against everything
seen so far.
output:
--- Program 22: Find Duplicates Using Hashing ---
Enter number of elements (values must be 0 to 999): 7
Enter the elements: 1 2 3 2 4 5 1
Duplicate elements: 2 1

title: Check whether a string is a palindrome
explanation:
Program 23: String Palindrome Check
Topic: Strings

Compares characters from both ends of the string moving inward
(str[0] with str[len-1], str[1] with str[len-2], ...). If every pair
matches, the string reads the same forwards and backwards.
output:
--- Program 23: String Palindrome Check ---
Enter a string: malayalam
"malayalam" is a palindrome

title: Pair with a given sum in a sorted array
explanation:
Program 24: Two Pointers - Pair With Given Sum
Topic: Two Pointers

On a SORTED array, one pointer starts at the left end, another at
the right end. If their sum is too small, the left pointer moves
right (to increase the sum); if too large, the right pointer moves
left (to decrease it). This finds a matching pair in a single pass
(O(n)) instead of checking every pair (O(n^2)).
output:
--- Program 24: Two Pointers - Pair With Given Sum ---
Enter number of elements: 6
Enter 6 elements in ascending (sorted) order: 1 2 3 4 6 8
Enter target sum: 10
Pair found: 2 + 8 = 10

title: Maximum sum subarray of size k (sliding window)
explanation:
Program 25: Sliding Window - Max Sum Subarray of Size k
Topic: Sliding Window

Rather than summing each window of size k from scratch, the window
"slides" one step at a time: subtract the element leaving the window
on the left, add the element entering on the right. This tracks the
max sum in O(n) instead of O(n*k).
output:
--- Program 25: Sliding Window - Max Sum Subarray of Size k ---
Enter number of elements: 8
Enter 8 elements: 2 1 5 1 3 2 7 1
Enter window size k: 3
Maximum sum of a subarray of size 3 is: 12

title: Binary search for a target in a sorted array
explanation:
Program 26: Binary Search
Topic: Binary Search

On a SORTED array, repeatedly check the middle element. If it is the
target, done. If the target is larger, search only the right half;
if smaller, search only the left half. Each step eliminates half the
remaining elements, giving O(log n) instead of a linear scan's O(n).
output:
--- Program 26: Binary Search ---
Enter number of elements: 6
Enter 6 elements in ascending (sorted) order: 2 4 6 8 10 12
Enter target value: 10
10 found at index 4

title: Array based min-heap: insert and extract-min
explanation:
Program 27: Min-Heap / Priority Queue
Topic: Heap / Priority Queue

A binary min-heap is stored in a plain array where, for index i, its
children live at 2*i+1 and 2*i+2. Inserting a value places it at the
end and "bubbles it up" by swapping with its parent while it's
smaller. Extracting the minimum removes the root (index 0), moves
the last element there, and "bubbles it down" by repeatedly swapping
with the smaller child until the heap property is restored. This
keeps the smallest value always accessible at the root in O(log n)
per operation.
output:
--- Program 27: Min-Heap / Priority Queue ---
How many numbers do you want to insert? 5
Enter 5 numbers: 5 3 8 1 9
1. Extract the minimum once
2. Extract all (prints numbers in sorted order)
Enter your choice: 2
Extracted order: 1 3 5 8 9

title: Print all permutations of a string
explanation:
Program 28: Permutations of a String
Topic: Backtracking

To generate all orderings, fix one character at the current
position, recursively permute the remaining characters, then swap
back ("backtrack") before trying a different character in that
position. This systematically explores every arrangement without
missing or repeating one.
output:
--- Program 28: Permutations of a String ---
Enter a short string (max 9 characters): abc
All permutations:
abc
acb
bac
bca
cba
cab

title: Activity selection (max non-overlapping tasks)
explanation:
Program 29: Activity Selection (Greedy)
Topic: Greedy

Sort all activities by their finish time. Then always pick the next
activity whose start time is not before the last selected activity's
finish time. Always choosing the activity that frees up time soonest
is the "greedy choice" - it can be proven to leave the most room for
future activities, giving the maximum possible count.
output:
--- Program 29: Activity Selection (Greedy) ---
Enter number of activities: 4
Enter start and finish time for each activity:
Activity 1 (start finish): 1 2
Activity 2 (start finish): 3 4
Activity 3 (start finish): 0 6
Activity 4 (start finish): 5 7
Selected activities (start, finish): (1, 2) (3, 4) (5, 7)
Maximum number of non-overlapping activities: 3

title: Basic bitwise operations demo
explanation:
Program 30: Bit Manipulation
Topic: Bit Manipulation

Three classic bitwise tricks: (1) num & 1 checks only the last bit -
0 means even, 1 means odd, faster than % 2. (2) Repeatedly checking
the last bit with & 1 and shifting right with >> counts how many 1
bits (set bits) a number has. (3) XOR-ing two variables three times
(a^=b; b^=a; a^=b;) swaps them without needing a third variable or
risking the overflow that plain addition/subtraction swapping can
have.
output:
--- Program 30: Bit Manipulation ---
Enter a number to check even/odd and count set bits: 12
12 is even (last bit is 0)
Number of set bits (1s) in 12 is: 2

Enter two numbers to swap using XOR: 5 9
Before swapping: a = 5, b = 9
After swapping : a = 9, b = 5

title: Merge overlapping intervals
explanation:
Program 31: Merge Overlapping Intervals
Topic: Intervals

Sort all intervals by their start time. Walk through them once: if
the current interval starts before or exactly when the last merged
interval ends, they overlap, so extend the last merged interval's
end if needed. Otherwise, the current interval starts a new group.
One pass after sorting is enough to merge everything correctly.
output:
--- Program 31: Merge Overlapping Intervals ---
Enter number of intervals: 4
Enter each interval as: start end
1 3
2 6
8 10
15 18
Merged intervals: [1, 6] [8, 10] [15, 18]

title: Climbing stairs (1-D DP)
explanation:
Program 32: Climbing Stairs (1-D DP)
Topic: Dynamic Programming (1-D)

To reach stair i, the last step taken was either from stair i-1 (a
1-step) or stair i-2 (a 2-step), so the number of ways to reach
stair i is ways[i-1] + ways[i-2] - the same recurrence as Fibonacci
(Program 16), but solved "bottom-up" by filling a table (ways[])
instead of recursive calls. This is the essence of dynamic
programming: build up answers to bigger subproblems from already
solved smaller ones.
output:
--- Program 32: Climbing Stairs (1-D DP) ---
Enter number of stairs: 5
Number of distinct ways to climb 5 stairs: 8
